questions.title: Does the 'relaxed' standing standard for procedural injuries still require a direct causal link between the agency's inaction and the plaintiff's concrete harm?
questions.question_body: The court mentions that when plaintiffs allege injury from a violation of a procedural right, courts 'relax' the requirements of imminence and redressability. However, the opinion states AFL fails even this relaxed standard. Specifically, why doesn't the relaxation allow for a more speculative chain of events? The court rejects AFL's argument that OSC *might* investigate, leading MSPB *might* sanction, leading DOJ *might* release records. Doesn't the 'relaxed' standard mean we don't need to prove that outcome is guaranteed, just probable enough? Why is this chain considered too speculative compared to typical environmental or zoning cases where relief often depends on multiple administrative steps?

questions.title: Can a statutory mandate to 'investigate' create a cognizable informational injury if the statute doesn't explicitly grant rights to specific reports or notifications?
questions.question_body: AFL argues that Section 1216 mandates OSC to investigate FOIA violations. They claim an informational injury because they aren't getting updates or results. The court says Section 1216 doesn't create an entitlement to receive information unless it triggers Section 1214 notice requirements. But isn't there a distinction between a right to *initiate* an investigation and a right to *information about* that investigation? If Congress wrote 'shall conduct an investigation,' shouldn't the complainant have a stake in knowing whether that duty was fulfilled? Why does the lack of explicit text granting 'notice rights' defeat the entire claim for informational standing here?

questions.title: How does the 'Heckler v. Chaney' presumption against judicial review of agency inaction interact with statutes using mandatory language like 'shall investigate'?
questions.question_body: The court cites *Heckler v. Chaney*, stating courts generally cannot compel agency enforcement discretion. Yet Section 1216(a)(3) uses the word 'shall... conduct an investigation.' Usually, mandatory language ('shall') removes agency discretion regarding whether to act. Does this mean the OSC actually had no choice but to investigate under 1216(a)(3), making their refusal unlawful regardless of discretion? Or does *Heckler* still shield them because even if they must start an investigation, deciding *how* far to go remains discretionary? I'm confused about whether 'mandatory investigation' overrides general prosecutorial discretion.

questions.title: Is Article III standing defeated solely by the presence of intervening independent actors (like MSPB or DOJ) in the causal chain, even if those actors are not parties?
questions.question_body: The core reason for dismissing AFL's first theory seems to be that redressing their injury requires speculating about what two non-party agencies (MSPB and DOJ) will do after OSC acts. Is this rule absolute? If I sue an agency for failing to enforce a law against another entity, am I automatically barred from standing whenever my desired outcome relies on that other entity changing its behavior voluntarily? How does this differ from cases where plaintiffs successfully challenge regulatory failures that indirectly cause market harms?

questions.title: What is the practical difference between being denied a 'procedural right in vacuo' versus having a procedural right attached to a concrete interest in this specific FOIA context?
questions.question_body: "Summers v. Earth Island Inst." says depriving someone of a procedural right without affecting a concrete interest is insufficient for standing ('procedural right in vacuo'). Here, AFL wants records (concrete interest) but claims injury because OSC won't help get them via procedure. The court says their injury isn't traceable to OSC because DOJ controls the records. So, was AFL's mistake trying to use OSC as a lever for DOJ compliance rather than seeking direct relief from DOJ? Did they fail because they sued the wrong defendant (OSC vs DOJ) despite claiming OSC has jurisdiction over FOIA violations?

questions.title: If Section 1216(c) allows OSC to act under sections 1214/1215 "in the same way," does that implicitly incorporate all Section 1214 notification requirements into Section 1216 investigations?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that under Section 1216(c), OSC can seek corrective action "in the same way" as prohibited personnel practices under Section 1214. Section 1214 includes specific notice requirements (e.g., informing complainants of progress). The Sixth Circuit (*Carson*) held OSC has discretion on whether to follow these notices during Section 1216 investigations. Does this conflict with D.C. Circuit precedent on statutory interpretation where "same way" usually means identical procedures apply unless specified otherwise? Is it possible Congress intended full parity in procedure but courts have narrowed it due to resource constraints or separation of powers concerns?
